headline: A randomized trial in China found that a WeChat chatbot helped ordinary people answer simulated respiratory-illness cases more accurately than web search did.
score_reason: Pool 6 kept: a large preregistered randomized study in a major journal, but simulated cases only and run by the chatbot's own developers.
importance_line: People who look up symptoms online get peer-reviewed evidence that a purpose-built chatbot beat web search at naming a likely respiratory condition, but the cases were simulated, urgency decisions improved less, and the chatbot's medical knowledge layer is owned by the authors' own research group, as the paper discloses.
summary: A peer-reviewed study in Nature Health reports that 2,400 adults without medical training at 24 Chinese health systems were randomly assigned, between April and June 2025, to answer simulated respiratory-illness cases with either LungDiag, a chatbot on the WeChat messaging app built on the GPT-4o model, or ordinary web search; the chatbot users were right 70.0% of the time against 55.4%. The gain came mainly from diagnosis questions (81.2% against 54.5%) and was smaller for triage, the judgment of how urgently to seek care (53.4% against 47.1%); the authors stress the cases were simulated, so the results do not show any effect on real-world care-seeking, diagnostic delay or health outcomes.
notes: Abstract, data availability and disclosure sections read from fulltext/C10-03.txt; the paper body is behind subscription. Publication date not shown in the page text (news feed: 5 Oct 2026). Source named as the journal, Nature Health, not the domain.
